highlights: Caspian waterfront grandeur beside Baku’s medieval walls and flame-lit skyline
description:
Four Seasons Hotel Baku stands on Neftchilar Avenue at Azneft Square, where central Baku meets the Caspian waterfront and the medieval walls of the Old City rise just steps away. The address is unusually cinematic: Icherisheher’s UNESCO-listed lanes, the seafront boulevard, the Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum and the Flame Towers all sit within the hotel’s immediate urban frame.

The 171 rooms and suites are housed in a purpose-built Beaux-Arts-style landmark with mansard roofs, arched windows and wrought-iron balconies that lend the property an old-European sense of ceremony. Inside, marble, chandeliers and polished classical detailing create a grand mood, while many rooms look either toward the Caspian Sea or back across the historic heart of the city. The scale feels formal without becoming remote, with balconies, high ceilings and generous public spaces keeping the waterfront light present.

Dining is centred on Zafferano, a light-filled Italian restaurant beneath vaulted ceilings, supported by Piazza lounge for tea and lighter fare, Bentley’s Whiskey Bar for cigars and cocktails, and seasonal terrace dining that brings the waterfront atmosphere into the hotel. The culinary mood is international but grounded by a setting that keeps Old Baku close at hand.

Wellness occupies the upper levels, with Jaleh Spa, hammam rituals, treatment rooms, a glass-roofed indoor pool and fitness facilities providing a calm counterpoint to the city outside. Meeting and event spaces add to the hotel’s civic scale, while family-friendly services suit longer stays. The defining pleasure is still its position between stone-walled heritage, museum culture, shopping streets and the bright Caspian horizon.

highlights: Serene Higashiyama sanctuary wrapped around an 800-year-old pond garden
description:
Four Seasons Hotel Kyoto lies in Higashiyama, one of Kyoto’s most atmospheric temple districts, with the slopes of the eastern hills behind it and cultural landmarks such as the Kyoto National Museum and Kiyomizu-dera within easy reach. Its defining feature is Shakusui-en, an 800-year-old pond garden that sits at the centre of the property and gives the hotel an unusually rooted sense of place.

The hotel combines 180 rooms, suites and residential suites with a restrained interpretation of Japanese design. Garden views, pale timber, screens, stone, carefully framed light and residential proportions create an urban retreat that feels quieter than its central location suggests. Some residential suites add private kitchens and expansive entertaining space, making the property feel part refined city hotel, part Kyoto residence.

Dining moves between precise Japanese craft and relaxed international polish. Sushi Ginza Onodera at Four Seasons Hotel Kyoto serves Edomae-style omakase with ingredients from local markets, Tokyo’s Toyosu Market and Hokkaido. EMBA KYOTO GRILL offers charcoal-grilled steak, seafood and garden-facing terrace dining, while Fuju Lounge shifts from daytime tea and afternoon tea to evening cocktails. Shakusui-tei, set by the pond garden, deepens the connection to Japanese tea, sake and the rituals of the garden.

The two-floor spa and wellness area includes seven treatment rooms, a 20-metre indoor pool, whirlpool and fitness centre, with therapies drawing on shiatsu, green tea and bamboo traditions. Cultural programming, garden-facing event spaces and occasional maiko performances add further texture, linking the hotel to Kyoto’s living arts rather than treating heritage as a backdrop. The quiet drama of the ancient pond remains the signature, especially as reflections shift through the seasons.

highlights: Beachfront West Bay retreat with Gulf views, bold dining and sculptural pools
description:
Four Seasons Hotel Doha occupies a prized position on the Corniche, facing the Arabian Gulf and the towers of West Bay from one of the capital’s most established luxury addresses. The setting balances city and resort: a private sandy beach and marina soften the urban skyline, while the Corniche gives direct access by car to Doha’s museums, Souq Waqif, Msheireb and the wider diplomatic district.

The 17-storey hotel has 237 rooms and suites, reimagined by Pierre-Yves Rochon with lighter sea-inspired colours, contemporary-classic furniture and Qatari references such as mother-of-pearl details and Arabic motifs. Floor-to-ceiling windows draw in the Gulf light, giving many rooms a clear sense of the water and skyline beyond. The result is polished but not anonymous, with the renovation tying the hotel more closely to Doha’s maritime setting.

Dining is one of the property’s strongest signatures. Nobu Doha sits dramatically above the Arabian Gulf with Chef Nobu Matsuhisa’s new-style Japanese cuisine, while Curiosa by Jean-Georges brings Latin energy to a terrace-led setting under Head Chef Shreyas Kadam. Nota Blu, tea lounges, poolside dining and a broader collection of restaurants and bars make the hotel as much a social address as a place to stay.

Wellness and leisure extend the resort feeling. The Spa and Wellness Centre has 11 treatment rooms with beachfront views, hydrotherapy facilities and a substantial fitness offering, while five pools include grotto-style options and family-friendly pools with slides. Tennis, beach time, marina views and family facilities round out a hotel that feels deliberately expansive without losing its Corniche polish.

hotel_name: Four Seasons Hotel Dubai International Financial Centre
highlights: Tailored DIFC hideaway with rooftop glamour, art galleries and Burj Khalifa views
description:
Four Seasons Hotel Dubai International Financial Centre anchors Gate Village in DIFC, Dubai’s polished financial and dining district. The location is more urban club than beach resort, placing galleries, restaurants and offices on the doorstep, with the Museum of the Future, Dubai Mall and Burj Khalifa all close by car. It is a particularly walkable base by Dubai standards, surrounded by the city’s densest concentration of polished restaurants and business addresses.

The boutique-scale hotel has 106 rooms, including 28 suites, with interiors by Tihany Design that favour custom finishes, glossy materials and a tailored contemporary mood. The scale is intimate for Dubai, and the best rooms use floor-to-ceiling glass to frame the city skyline; the Penthouse Suite opens to 180-degree views that include Burj Khalifa. The atmosphere is closer to a private members’ club than a conventional resort.

Dining reflects DIFC’s social rhythm. MINA Brasserie brings Michael Mina’s French-Mediterranean brasserie cooking to a lively room and terrace, while Penrose Lounge moves from refined afternoon tea to cocktails in a more residential setting. Luna Dubai, the rooftop bar, adds skyline drama with an Asian-inspired menu and a terrace designed for evening city views; Glasswater extends the mood to poolside dining.

Wellness is compact but polished, with Pearl Spa and Wellness, five light-filled treatment rooms, a fitness centre and a glass-walled rooftop pool that gives the hotel much of its visual identity. Meeting spaces and business services suit the district, yet the property’s stronger character lies in its small-scale glamour: a precise, design-led Four Seasons base embedded in one of Dubai’s most urbane neighbourhoods.

highlights: Elevated safari lodge overlooking elephant-frequented waterholes in the Central Serengeti
description:
Four Seasons Safari Lodge Serengeti sits inside Serengeti National Park in northern Tanzania, deep in a landscape defined by open plains, kopjes, seasonal migration routes and year-round wildlife. Its central Serengeti position gives the lodge direct access to game drives and the wider park ecosystem, while the property itself is arranged above an active watering hole that draws animals close to the lodge.

The lodge has 77 rooms, suites and villas, including five free-standing private villas. Interiors blend contemporary comfort with African materials and warm safari references, framing the savannah through terraces, outdoor showers, plunge pools in selected categories and broad windows. The scale is larger than many safari camps, yet the architecture keeps a strong visual connection to the plains and the movements of wildlife below.

Safari is the core experience, with expert driver-guides leading half-day and full-day game drives in search of lions, elephants, cheetahs, leopards, buffalo and the herds that move through the Serengeti. Hot-air balloon safaris, bush dinners, picnic outings, conservation activities and family programming add variety without diluting the focus on wildlife. Depending on season and movement, the broader region can also bring the drama of wildebeest and zebra migration into reach.

Back at the lodge, Kula’s Restaurant, Boma Grill, Maji Bar and terrace dining provide flexible places to gather after the day’s drives. The free-form infinity pool overlooks the watering hole, while the spa uses freestanding treatment pavilions and private terrace baths to create a slower rhythm between safari outings. The result is a highly comfortable wilderness base where the spectacle of the Serengeti remains constantly visible, even between scheduled drives.
